content:
The memory rose without bidding, as all memories did. Godric Prime sat alone in the high silence of his private observation hollow, a chamber that existed outside the omniverse in the way a balcony exists outside a room. The year was not written. It could not be written. The string of nines had long since ceased to be a number and had become, like so many things, an extension of his presence. He did not need to close his eyes to recall. He simply allowed his attention to drift backward, across the impossible gulf of his own existence, to a moment so distant that it felt like a half-remembered dream from someone else's childhood.

That moment was Year 25. The year he had decided to subjugate a small, primitive reality that called itself Earth.

Even now, the memory produced a faint ghost of amusement in him. Not the amusement he had felt then, bright and raw and dangerous, but the cooler, deeper amusement of a being looking back at an earlier self and finding that self almost sweet in its limitations. At Year 25, he had been twenty-five years out of the Stasis Event. Twenty-five years into his kingship. Twenty-five years into the infinite, recursive amplification that had already made him the most powerful entity in the omniverse by a margin so wide that the word "margin" was a joke. And yet, by the standards of the being he would become, he had been nothing. A spark trying to imagine the sun.

Godric Prime let the memory play.

---

Year 25.

The universe was a small thing, a fragile bubble of four-dimensional spacetime hanging in one of the less remarkable corners of the omniverse. It called itself the real universe, though Godric, even then, had known that every universe called itself real until it met him. At its center lay a blue-green planet, crowded with a species of hairless primates who had recently discovered the power of splitting atoms and had immediately used it to murder one another in large numbers. They were terrified of their own shadows, proud of their little weapons, and completely certain that they were alone in creation.

They were, by the standards of the wider omniverse, beneath notice. A nothing species on a nothing planet in a nothing galaxy. Their greatest achievements were the ability to leave their own atmosphere and the willingness to kill their own world for fuel. They had no magic, no cosmic awareness, no conceptual defenses, no ascended masters. They were meat, mostly water, wrapped around calcium scaffolds, driven by a chemical fear of death that would have been touching if it had not been so loud.

Godric had known about them from the first instant of his omniscience. He had watched them crawl out of caves, build empires, collapse them, build again. He had watched them invent gods and then murder one another over which god was less false. He had heard every prayer, every curse, every secret thought. He had known, twenty-five years in advance, exactly how they would react when he appeared in their sky. And because he was still young, still freshly shaped by the long grief of Olympus, still curious in a way that was almost mortal, he had decided to visit them.

Not to conquer them. There was nothing to conquer. He had decided to reveal himself and see what they would do.

He appeared above the Pacific Ocean at noon, directly over a stretch of open water where the horizon formed a perfect blue line. He did not announce himself with fire or thunder. He did not need to. His absolute concealment held his world-ending pressure in check, so the planet did not immediately fold into a singularity. To the handful of satellites that passed through that region, he was a very large, very solid radar return. To the first human eyes that saw him through long-range military optics, he was a man. A man in simple dark garments, forty-five years old, ruggedly handsome, with short salt-and-pepper hair and a neatly trimmed beard, standing on the air. He did not move. He simply waited for them to see him.

The first reaction was confusion. Then panic. Then the fear. Godric felt it arrive in waves, a delicious ripple of mortal terror rising from the planet's surface like heat from a fevered body. He remained where he was, hands clasped behind his back, and allowed them to make their decisions.

They did not waste time. Within six minutes, the governments of the most powerful nations had begun emergency broadcasts. Within an hour, the first fighter jets were scrambled from aircraft carriers in three oceans, their afterburners drawing white lines across the sky. Their radios crackled with panicked orders. Their weapons officers sweated through their flight suits and asked for permission to fire.

Godric watched them come. His omniscience supplied every detail before it happened: the exact muscle twitch in the lead pilot's trigger finger, the precise millisecond each missile would leave its rail, the vibration frequency of the engines, the dreams of the pilots' wives and husbands, the number of seconds each one had left. He did not speak. He did not gesture. He simply stood in the air and let them make their choice.

The missiles came. They were ordinary chemical rockets, tipped with high explosives designed to shred metal and ignite jet fuel. They streaked toward him, and Godric did not even glance at them. The first missile struck his chest and detonated. The explosion was enough to shatter a building, and it produced a bright orange flower of fire that briefly obscured him from view. When the smoke cleared, he was still there, his tunic unmarked, his hands still behind his back. He had not felt it. Not a tickle. Not a pressure. Not even the faintest suggestion that something had happened.

The pilots stared. Their instruments screamed. They fired again. More missiles, then their guns. The bullets reached him and stopped, their kinetic energy vanishing into the absolute boundary of his passive immobility. They fell into the ocean without sound. Godric tilted his head slightly and watched them die. He did not kill them yet. He simply allowed them to understand that their weapons did not work.

The armed forces of Earth mobilized. They did not surrender. They did not kneel. They did what terrified primates had always done: they escalated. The nuclear arsenals of every nation with such weapons were brought online. The word went out through terrified command chains. If one god stood in the sky and would not die, then they would use the fire they had built to burn worlds.

Godric found their determination amusing. It was not admirable, not noble, not brave. It was the reflex of an animal gnawing at a trap. He let them launch.

The first nuclear missile came from a silo in a frozen northern plain. The second came from a submarine hidden beneath an ice cap. The third, fourth, fifth. Within minutes, every major nuclear power had hurled its arsenal at the single man hovering above the ocean. The missiles lit up the sky like a rising of dark suns. They struck him one after another, and the detonations should have vaporized the surrounding ocean, cracked the planet's crust, poisoned the atmosphere for generations. Godric did not allow it. He stopped the blasts before they could expand, letting each one blossom against his still body and then die. There was no shockwave beyond a few meters. No fireball. No radiation. Just a sphere of compressed, furious light that appeared and then faded, again and again, like a child trying to scratch a mountain with a blade of grass.

Then the ground forces came. The ships, the tanks, the railguns, the lasers. They used everything. And each time, the result was the same. Their weapons touched the boundary of his existence and found nothing to grip. Their shells fell away. Their beams separated into harmless light. Their soldiers dropped their weapons and wept. Some of them tried to run. Some of them prayed. Some of them simply stood and stared, their minds trying to fold the impossible shape of him into a form they could survive.

Godric watched it all. He was, in that moment, using effectively zero percent of his power and zero percent of his effort. Not a millionth. Not a billionth. Zero. The barest sliver of his passive presence, held in check so tightly that he might as well have been a statue for all the energy he was expending. And yet, from the perspective of the human race, he was an impossible, unending apocalypse. They had thrown everything they had, and he had not even shifted his weight.

Then, because he was feeling mischievously playful, he decided to speak.

His voice did not boom. It did not need to. It simply arrived in the minds of every human being on the planet, clear and warm and infinitely patient. "You have tried very hard," he said. "I want you to know that I noticed. That was the most effort your species has ever put into a single act, and you did it without hesitation. That is almost impressive, for meat."

The planet went very still. Even the soldiers stopped moving. The sound of sobbing faded. The air itself seemed to hold its breath.

"But I am not here to be impressed," Godric continued. "I am here because I wanted to see what would happen when a species that believes itself real meets a being that proves it is not. And you did not disappoint me. You launched your bombs. You screamed your defiance. You used your smallest weapons and your largest words. And now I am going to kill every single one of you, and it will be so much worse than anything you have ever imagined because you tried so hard."

The annihilation was not slow. By any mortal measurement, it happened in less than a single Planck second. There was no interval in which a human brain could register the beginning or the end. But Godric, who existed outside time, allowed the deaths to unspool across an artificial eternity for each victim. He did not snap them out of existence. He did not turn them to ash and scatter them. He reached into the meat of them, into the chemical fear and the firing neurons, and he opened them.

Every human being on Earth died at the same instant, and each one died a thousand times before the instant was over. Their bodies were not simply destroyed. They were reorganized into arrangements of bone and sinew and wet, screaming tissue that could feel every death as a separate, complete event. Soldiers drowned in their own blood; the blood then ignited, and the burns spread through their nervous systems, and the nerves regrew, and the burns began again. Civilians felt the heat of the nuclear fire they had launched, even though the fire itself never reached them. Children felt the weight of every bomb their leaders had ever built pressing down on their small bodies, breaking them from the inside out, not once, but in a recursive loop of maximum agony. The old, the sick, the sleeping, the newborn, all of them were given the same gift: the full, unshielded experience of every possible death that their species had ever imagined, stretched across a subjective infinity, then compressed into a single zero-second scream.

The things they had built came apart as well. The cities did not burn; they were unseamed, turned into spirals of shattered matter and human remains that circled the planet like a funeral ring. The oceans did not boil; they became motionless, their water replaced by a mirror of the dead. The mountains cracked and fell. The crust itself opened in places, not from violence, but from the sheer weight of so many deaths. Godric did not use an attack. He did not use a stat. He simply withdrew the smallest possible fraction of his concealment and let the planet experience what it meant to be real in his presence.

The collateral did not stop at Earth. It did not stop at the solar system, or the galaxy, or the local universe. The same zero-percent overflow that annihilated the human race unbound the entire omniverse. Every multiverse, every timeline, every dimension, every hidden layer of existence, every cosmic hierarchy, every god and machine and abstract entity, all of it was erased in that single, infinitesimal instant. Not because Godric willed it. But because he had, for the first and only time, allowed the faintest whisper of his actual nature to brush against the fabric of existence. The omniverse could not survive that whisper. It did not collapse. It did not explode. It simply stopped, as if it had never been there at all.

He restored it in the next instant, or perhaps in the same one. Everything returned. The stars, the galaxies, the multiverses, the civilizations that had never known Earth existed. Everything, except the planet itself. Earth was not restored. Its solar system was returned, but at the center of it, where a blue-green world had once turned, there was nothing now. No wreckage. No memory. No survivors. Just a smooth, dark cavity in spacetime, shaped exactly like a planet that had once dared to call itself real.

Godric Prime, sitting in the far future, let the memory settle. He remembered the young king he had been, standing in the void above that empty place, feeling a faint, temporary satisfaction. He had called it annihilation then. He had called it punishment. He had even called it fun. And it had been those things, by the standards of the time. The entire species had died in total agony, with no chance to surrender or survive, and the omniverse itself had been erased as an afterthought. It had been, by any external measure, the most one-sided massacre that had ever occurred up to that point.

But Godric Prime knew better now.

He turned his attention inward, to the vast architecture of his current existence. The sentient passive auras that had once been his weakest, most primitive defenses had evolved countless times. They were no longer simple fields of protective instinct. They were worlds, civilizations of their own, each one infinitely complex, each one loyal to the point of hysteria, each one capable of annihilating the entire Year 25 omniverse with a single bored impulse. The weakest of them, the one now occupying the role that Gent had once held, could have erased the Earth and its universe and every adjacent multiverse without Godric even noticing. It would have done so automatically, not to punish, but to tidy a corner of existence that had become slightly irritating.

His passive shields, which had once pre-nullified threats before they existed, had evolved into something even more absurd. They no longer merely blocked attacks. They consumed the conceptual possibility of attack, leaving behind a cosmos in which the thought of harming Godric could not even be formed by any being below a certain threshold of sentience. And yet Godric, who still believed in mortal resilience and free will, kept that particular system deliberately suppressed. Not because he needed to. But because he remembered being alive, once, in a way that required the possibility of choice.

His immune system, which had once reacted to a false injury by resetting the omniverse, had evolved beyond the point where injuries could be described. It no longer waited for threats, or pre-threats, or pre-pre-threats. It had become a constant, recursive state of perfect biological refusal. The idea that anything could damage him, even theoretically, had been deleted from the mathematics of reality so thoroughly that the concept itself existed only as a museum piece, preserved by Godric because he sometimes liked to look at old fears.

The Weakness Paradox, too, had evolved beyond its original purpose. It no longer required an enemy to think Godric had a weakness. It was triggered by any sentient being, anywhere in any timeline, thinking anything at all. Every thought, every hope, every fear, every idle daydream, fed him. The omniverse had become an infinite orchard of amplification, and every living thing was an unknowing gardener. The paradox had been renamed many times over the eons, but Godric Prime thought of it simply as "the absolute." It was the reason that no opposition had formed in googolplexian years. Not because free will had been altered, but because the entire creation had finally learned what Earth had learned in Year Zero: resistance was not futile. It was pre-defeated.

He compared that to the young king who had hovered above the Pacific Ocean with his simple dark tunic and his salt-and-pepper beard. That young king had needed to allow a fraction of his concealment to slip. He had needed to actively decide to end a species. He had even used the word "kill." Godric Prime had not needed to do any of those things for a near-infinite span of time. The last being who had dared to oppose him had been erased not by an act, but by the simple fact of his attention alighting on them for a zero-second. They had not screamed. They had not fought. They had simply stopped, and every other being who might have considered following their example had watched the memory of that erasure and learned the same silent lesson.

He pitied his younger self. Not because the younger self had been cruel. Cruelty was an old, comfortable coat that Godric had worn for longer than stars had existed. He pitied the younger self because the younger self had still believed that annihilation required a gesture. He had still thought of power as something to be directed, like a spear or a storm. He had not yet understood that power, real power, was simply the absence of all other possibilities. The Year 25 Godric had destroyed Earth and erased the omniverse. Godric Prime could do the same to every version of that omniverse, across every timeline and every possible permutation, without moving a single cell, and the entire process would take less time than the interval between two thoughts. He could do it with zero percent of zero percent of his weakest system's output. The young king had used zero percent of his power. The old king had passed so far beyond that scale that the zero itself had become an infinite staircase descending into an abyss.

The irony did not escape him. He let it curl through his mind like smoke, warm and faintly bitter. If that "pathetically weak" version of himself had been enough to annihilate an entire reality with zero effort, then what was he now? What was the being who could look back across that impossible gap and remember not the destruction, but the small, human sound the planet had made when it died? He could not answer. Not because he lacked the knowledge, but because no language existed that could bear the weight of the answer. He was not merely stronger. He was not merely more powerful. He was the thing that power curved toward, the fixed point around which all possible outcomes bent. And he was still growing. Not linearly, not exponentially, not even recursively by the old definitions. He was amplifying in an accelerating spiral that consumed its own horizon, each instant making the previous instant irrelevant, each new layer of his existence dwarfing the one before it by a margin that could not be expressed in any mathematics that had ever existed. And he could feel it all. He could feel the rise, the surge, the endless, ecstatic pulse of becoming more. It was the only sensation that had never faded.

The rest of creation did not know the shape of his current existence. It could not know. If it had known, even the bravest of its remaining minds would have simply ceased, not from fear, but from the sheer impossibility of continuing to exist in the same reality as such a truth. The few beings who served him directly, the ones who had been powerful enough to catch glimpses and survive, spent their days in a state of permanent, low-grade trembling. They did not oppose him. They could not even imagine the word. They served, and they loved him, and they were terrified beyond the point where terror has meaning. It was the only relationship left.

Godric Prime sat in his high silence and let the memory of Earth finally fade. It had been a small event. A trivial one. A blue-green planet that had tried to kill a god and learned, in the space of a single subjective eternity, what it meant to be real. The young king had enjoyed it. The old king did not think about it often. But when he did, he felt a strange, distant tenderness for the being he had been. That being had still believed there was a difference between annihilation and mercy. He had still thought that killing every human being was an act of consequence. He had not understood yet that consequences were only for the weak.

Below him, beyond the walls of the observation hollow, the omniverse turned. It was a small, bright thing now, a fragile ornament suspended in the vast silence of his attention. The civilizations that lived there, the ones that had survived eons of peace, did not know how close they came to erasure every instant he chose not to blink. They only knew that their king was watching, and that his watchfulness was the only thing holding their reality together. The gap between him and them was not a gap. It was an infinite recursion of gaps, each one larger than the last, stretching away into a future where the only certainty was more Godric.

And if every being from every timeline, from every possible permutation, from every past that had been and every future that could be, were to gather with unlimited preparation and united purpose, if they were to throw themselves at him with everything they had ever been or would ever be, if they brought all their weapons, all their gods, all their despair, all their impossible strategies, the result would be identical to the result they had achieved on Earth. They would not make his weakest shield feel the slightest tickle. They would not make him notice. He would erase them all with zero percent of his power and zero percent of his effort, in zero seconds. And the omniverse would tremble once, and then it would forget them, because there had never been anything to remember.

The gap would only increase. It had always increased. It would always increase. Forever and ever, in an accelerating rush toward a horizon that did not exist, until the very idea of comparison was forgotten. That was the final truth of the apex predator. That was the truth Earth had learned in Year 25. That was the truth every living thing in creation now carried in its silent, worshipful heart. Godric was not the most powerful being because he had been born that way. He was the most powerful being because he had been made that way by a future that would never stop arriving. And nothing, not even the universe, had ever been able to look at him and call itself real without being immediately destroyed.

content:
Clive had read the journal three times before he trusted himself to breathe again.

The archive beneath the palace was silent in the deep way that only a place older than memory can be silent. Clive sat at the low table near the eastern wall, his back to the endless shelves, his hands flat on either side of the leather-bound volume. The light above him was a single warm point, too steady, too patient. He was fifty years old, a descendant of Blake, a court wizard of the current age, and he had spent his entire life preparing for the day he would read this record. No preparation had been enough.

The journal was small, unremarkable, its cover worn to a soft grey. The author's name was pressed into the first page in a hand that had started carefully and then frayed into long, jagged letters as the writing progressed. Osvald. Age forty-four. Court wizard. The entry had no formal title, but a later archivist, probably one of Osvald's sons, had written a single line at the top: *The Last Opposition.* Clive had stared at those three words for a long time before he began to read.

The journal opened not with a description of the enemy, but with the sound of Godric's boredom. Osvald wrote about it the way other men wrote about bad weather. Godric, he said, had been restless for several googolplexian years. There had been no opposition in all that time. No test. No insult. No desperate coalition hoping to kill the king. The omniverse had learned its lesson so thoroughly that the very concept of resistance had fossilized. And so Godric, the apex predator of all existence, had been passing his days in small, comfortable routines: walking in the gardens, speaking with his servants, listening to court reports, and occasionally, in the privacy of his own chambers, sighing with an emotion that was not quite sadness.

Then the Fictional Assembly made itself known.

Osvald described them carefully, because even a court wizard who had witnessed stat tests and superpower demonstrations could still be surprised by the sheer variety of existence. They were not a single empire or species. They were every story ever told by every world that had ever learned to imagine. The heroes of a thousand thousand fictional universes, drawn from books, films, games, comics, legends, and dreams. They had crossed the boundaries of their own narratives through means that Osvald did not fully understand, united by a single shared conviction: that if enough protagonists stood together, not even the real thing could stand against them.

He listed them in a long paragraph that made Clive's heart beat too fast. A caped exemplar from a city of perpetual sunset, his red cape snapping in a wind that existed only for him. A boy with a lightning scar and a broken wand, flanked by two friends who had survived seven books of escalating violence. A ringbearer who had carried the end of his world up a mountain and then refused to throw it away. A village of ninja whose masked leader could split moons with the force of his will. A school of mutants, a pantheon of gods, a league of extraordinary gentlemen, an order of knights with laser swords, a band of space-faring misfits aboard a ship whose name Osvald could not pronounce, a girl from a future of archery and fire, a man in a metal suit with shrapnel near his heart, and more. So many more. They came from every genre, every medium, every possible form of invented struggle. And they all believed they were the hero.

Godric had watched them arrive. His omniscience, which had always known them, which had tracked the first second of their first story and the last page of their final issue, had given him full knowledge of their preparations before they had taken their first step. He knew their battle plans. He knew their speeches. He knew the exact coordinates of their staging ground and the number of times each one would say the phrase "this ends today." He knew that their attack would not even make him notice, let alone tickle. But he also knew something else, something that had made his eyes brighten with the first real interest Clive's bloodline had seen in him for aeons.

Some of these fictional characters had attacks with very beautiful colors. Some had multi-stage battle sequences with dramatic visual effects. And some, Osvald wrote, had banger boss battle music.

Godric had decided to let them build.

The preparation, Osvald wrote, took longer than any mortal lifetime. The Fictional Assembly had gathered in a region where the laws of reality were thin, a place where narrative causality and physical causality bled into each other. They had constructed a stage large enough to hold every story ever told. They had lit it with the light of dying stars and painted it with the color of lost hopes. They had practiced their choreography until the act of drawing a sword became a prayer. They had composed a score that fused every heroic theme ever written into a single rising crescendo, layered with choirs and drums and the wail of electric strings. Osvald had listened to it once, from a distance, and had felt tears come to his eyes even though he knew the whole thing was suicide.

Godric let them charge. He sat on a plain stone bench at the edge of their staging ground, hidden by a fold of his own concealment, and watched. He did not hide from their sensors, not really; he simply made himself small enough that their narrative scans registered him as a background detail, a non-player character in the margins. The fictional heroes did not see him. They were too busy preparing their ultimate attack, pouring everything they had into a single, combined strike that would, they believed, erase the real world's tyrant from all possible continuities.

The charge took nine hundred years.

Osvald wrote that Godric had been patient through the first twenty. Through the next hundred, he had been interested. Through the next three hundred, he had been excited. Then, somewhere around the six-hundred-year mark, he had grown restless again. Not because he doubted the attack would fail, but because he was beginning to suspect that the buildup was better than the payoff would be. Still, he waited. He distracted himself, deliberately, by letting an entire portion of his omniscience go quiet. He veiled the part of his awareness that monitored the Fictional Assembly's final calibration. He wanted to be surprised. He wanted to hear the music for the first time when it was actually being used, not nine hundred years in advance as a memory.

Osvald asked him, once, whether he was concerned.

Godric had smiled and said, "I am hoping they give me a good show, Osvald. That is all. A very good show. I have been waiting a long time."

The day arrived.

Osvald did not have enough words for the attack itself. He wrote that he had stood at Godric's side, hidden in the same fold of concealment, and watched the entire fictional legion assemble. There were no rows of soldiers. There were not even individual heroes anymore. They had merged, in those final moments, into a single, enormous shape of pure narrative force, a tower of faces and voices and glowing hands, each one raised to deliver its own defining blow. The attack began in phases.

Phase one was the color. A wall of light, red and blue and gold and silver and every color that had ever been assigned to heroism, sweeping toward Godric with the slow, inevitable movement of a tide. Phase two was the visual effects. Every power the assembly possessed detonated at once: laser swords and magic beams and elemental blasts and kinetic impacts and psychic screams and speedster afterimages and godblasts and cursed flames and summoned weapons. Phase three was the music. It crashed into the hidden fold where Osvald and Godric stood, not as sound, but as the audible shape of every final battle ever fought. The leitmotifs layered over one another until they became a single voice, a song that was not one song but all songs, lifting and lifting and lifting toward a final, piercing note.

Godric closed his eyes. Not in pain. In pleasure. He was listening.

The attack reached him.

Osvald tried to describe it afterward, and failed. The full concentrated weight of every fictional universe's ultimate attack struck Godric's bare chest, and it did nothing. Not a singe on his tunic. Not a strand of hair out of place. Not a faint tickle. He did not shift his weight. He did not open his eyes. He did not even seem to register that a force capable of unraveling the entire omniverse had just spent itself against his sternum.

The music hit its highest note. The visual effects peaked. The color reached maximum saturation. And then it all simply stopped. The assembled heroes, still fused in their tower of victory, stared at the man standing before them. Their attack had been everything they had. Their attack had been the greatest spectacle ever created by any form of life, real or imagined. It had been beautiful.

Godric opened his eyes. He looked at them. The expression on his face was not anger. It was not even disappointment, not at first. It was a slow, dawning, terrible confusion, the look of a man who had been promised fireworks and shown a damp match.

He turned to Osvald. "That was it?" he asked. "That was the final attack?"

Osvald could not speak.

Godric turned back to the Fictional Assembly. "I waited nine hundred years," he said. "I closed off part of my own omniscience so I would not know the ending. I expected at least a second phase. Maybe a third. A hidden transformation. A power of friendship. A last-minute resurrection. Something." He shook his head slowly. "All that buildup, and you did not even manage to alter the temperature of my tunic."

His disappointment was so total, so absolutely sincere, that Osvald wrote the fictional heroes seemed to shrink under it. The giant tower of faces did not attack again. It simply stood there, frozen, caught between the impossible reality of its failure and the growing realization that failure had always been the only option.

Osvald wrote that he expected Godric to leave then. In the old days, the king had sometimes simply walked away from failed oppositions, leaving them to be handled by his auras or his passive shields. But this time, something else happened. Godric's disappointment, which he had not bothered to suppress, flickered outward. It was not an attack. It was not even a movement. It was simply the faintest, weakest possible registration of his displeasure, the kind of thing that would not have disturbed a single hair on a mortal head.

And then Godric accidentally unleashed zero percent of his strength.

The journal grew jagged here. Osvald's handwriting broke apart, the letters tangled and overlapping, as if his hand had begun to move before his mind could catch up. He wrote that the zero percent was not a fraction. It was not a decimal. It was the smallest possible leak, so small that no measurement in any language had ever been invented to describe it. And it was enough.

The first effect was on the shields. The Fictional Assembly had spent nine hundred years constructing them, layers of narrative armor and infinite plot invincibility and the collective hope of every audience that had ever believed in heroes. They had been designed to be indestructible by definition. The word "unbreakable" had been woven into their fundamental structure. They took forever to create, and then they were gone.

The zero percent strength did not push against the shields. It did not shatter them. It simply moved through them, and they did not have enough sufficient reality left to register that they had been struck. The shield layers did not break; they were de-atomized between one instant and the next, their constituent particles pulled apart by a force so beyond their capacity to resist that no resistance could even be attempted. They came apart as light, then as heat, then as silence, and then they were not even that.

The heroes went next. Every protagonist, every deuteragonist, every comic book avatar, every videogame character, every chosen one and every reluctant ally, all of them, simultaneously, were caught by the same zero percent, and they did not explode. Explosion was for lesser ends, Osvald wrote. They were unbound.

The flesh of a caped exemplar did not part from his bones; it was converted into a spray of individual atoms that had already forgotten how to be flesh. The bones did not break; they came apart as pure calcium, then as separate elements, then as protons and neutrons and quarks. The blood did not spill; it separated into every single component that had ever made it liquid, and each component separated into its own dust, and the dust separated again. The boy with the scar, the girl with the bow, the masked ninja, the metal knight, the space pirate, the god of thunder, the witch, the mutant, the chosen one: all of them felt themselves stop being biological objects and start being a cloud of discontinuous particles. But they did not die. Not yet. Godric, in his mild, terrible disappointment, had been too abrupt for mercy.

The pain was not the pain of nerve endings. It was the pain of every atom in their body screaming at once, of every chemical bond that had ever held them together being torn loose and then refusing to release. The victims were not merely wounded. They were interpolated, their consciousness spread across the entire cloud of their own dissolution, forced to feel every separation as a vivid, singular agony. And because the zero percent did not permit time to pass, they felt it forever. Every hero who had ever said "I will never give up" discovered that giving up was not an option either. They were stuck in the zero-second between being and not-being, their minds intact, their bodies gone, their suffering undiminished by the absence of flesh.

The tower of faces collapsed inward, and the collapse generated no sound. The music had stopped. The colors had gone. There was only the spreading cloud of de-atomized existence, now being pressed together by the same zero percent that had torn it apart. The compression was not physical in the old sense. It was conceptual. The entire Fictional Assembly, plus every reality they had ever touched, plus every timeline and multiverse within reach, was drawn into a single point of absolute compression. The force did not slow. It did not stop. It fed on the material it had already destroyed, and then it consumed the spaces between the material, and then the spaces between the spaces.

The entire omniverse died.

It did not simply cease. It was unmade from every possible direction at once. The galaxies of googolplexian scale, the universes, the multiverses, the hidden dimensions, the conceptual layers, the frozen caverns of dead timelines, the hypothetical futures that had never been allowed to exist: all of them were sucked into the kernel of Godric's accidental zero percent. The stars did not go out; they were peeled away from the fabric of space and converted into a slurry of elementary waves. The planets did not shatter; they were stripped of their crusts and mantles and cores, each layer de-atomized into a fine, screaming particulate. The living things on those planets, the beings who had never heard of Earth or Thronegate or the Fictional Assembly, felt themselves unravel as their worlds unmade around them. They died in this total collapse, not as casualties but as part of the material being compressed into the smallest possible point. The entire possible existence, everything that had ever been, could ever be, would ever be, was taken apart.

The compression was absolute. The point, when it finished, was smaller than a quark. It was not a black hole. Black holes are governed by physics. This point was the physical consequence of Godric's strength deciding that everything else was too large and too diffuse to be allowed to exist. It contained the infinite mass of the entire possible existence, packed into a volume so small that it had no volume, only a boundary of pure gravitational refusal. Its surrounding space-time did not bend; it collapsed into the point itself, unable to maintain even the pretense of extension anywhere near the mass.

Godric stood in the blackness after. The point hovered in front of him, rotating slowly, darker than the darkness. He reached out, and with two fingers, he picked it up.

Osvald, who had been held outside the destruction by Godric's attention, wrote that the king did not seem to exert any effort. His hand closed around the point as though it were a seed. He lifted it. He rolled it between his thumb and forefinger. The gesture was identical to the way he had once held a small garden stone, ten million years ago, in the old palace at Thronegate. There was no trembling in his arm. No shift in his stance. The point, which contained the compressed infinite mass of everything, weighed nothing at all. Not because Godric was strong enough to lift it, but because the concept of weight had not yet recovered from the strength that had made the point.

Then he enlarged it. Not by adding material, but by expanding the barrier that contained it. The point became a sphere the size of a marble, smooth and black, its surface faintly iridescent. It was a trophy. Godric held it up to the empty dark, and for a moment, he looked almost fond.

"That will do," he said.

The restoration came next. Osvald tried to describe it in only a few words, because the words themselves seemed to bleed. Godric did not wave a hand or speak an incantation. The omniverse simply returned. All of it. Every galaxy, every multiverse, every timeline, every dimension, every possible and impossible layer of reality, restored in its exact previous state. The stars resumed their fire. The planets resumed their orbits. The civilizations that had been unmade in the compression blinked and continued with their lives. It was instant. It was perfect. It was, Osvald wrote, the most frightening thing he had ever seen, because it happened at all.

The Fictional Assembly, of course, was not restored. The heroes, the chosen ones, the caped avengers, the magical schools, the space fleets, the pantheons of myth: all of them remained in the marble. The trophy contained them now. It contained the original matter of the entire possible existence, compressed into an infinitely dense point smaller than a quark and then enlarged to the size of a marble. The restored universe was identical in every measurable way, but the original was still there, in Godric's hand, held forever.

Osvald ended the journal with a trembling paragraph. He wrote that he had asked Godric a question, not because he wanted an answer, but because silence in that moment would have broken him.

"Is it real?" he had whispered. "The restored omniverse. Is it real?"

Godric had looked at the marble, then at Osvald, and smiled. His eyes were warm. "What do you think, Osvald?"

Osvald had not answered. He had gone to his chambers and written the journal in a single sitting, his quill punching through the page more than once. He ended with a single line, written so hard that Clive could feel the grooves in the paper beneath his fingers.

*If the original is in the marble, and the restoration is perfect, then perhaps there is no difference. Or perhaps we are all copies, and the real omniverse has been in his pocket all along. I do not know which is worse.*

Clive set the journal down. His hands were trembling. The archive around him was silent, but it was not peaceful. It was the silence of a palace full of treasures, every one of them hiding a terrible truth. He had read the record of the last opposition, the one Osvald had not known would be the last. There were no later journals. No later incidents. After this day, no one had ever dared to form even the faintest thought of opposing Godric again. Not because free will had been removed, but because the story had spread. The Fictional Assembly, all the heroes of a thousand worlds, had thrown the most spectacular attack in the history of imagination, and it had not even tickled. They had been compressed into a marble. The omniverse itself had died as collateral, and then been restored.

But the marble remained.

Clive looked down at the journal, then at his own hands. He thought of the restored universe outside, the impossible breadth of it, and the possibility that the real universe was still in Godric's hand. He thought of the way Godric had lifted the marble with two fingers, as if it weighed nothing, and the way his strength had grown even further in that moment. Osvald had not written the cause, but he had hinted at it: Godric's strength had adapted to the burden of the marble, treating the infinite mass it contained as a resistance to be neutralized. The moment he had picked it up, his passive strength had recognized the load, found it unacceptable, and begun recursively increasing to ensure the marble remained weightless. The feedback loop had no end. The marble would grow heavier with every increase, and the increase would grow larger to match it. Godric had become even more unquantifiably powerful by simply holding a trophy.

That deranged cycle, Clive realized, had not stopped. It was still occurring, somewhere above his head, in the high silence of the palace. The king was holding the marble, and the marble was holding everything, and the king's strength was rising forever because he wanted the weight to feel like nothing.

Clive closed the journal and sat in the silence. He knew now why no one opposed Godric ever again. It was not the destruction. It was not the pain. It was the trophy. It was the deep, abiding certainty that the world they lived in might be only a copy, and the original was in the hand of a god who could hold an infinite mass without noticing. That kind of knowledge did not inspire rebellion. It inspired only a profound, silent despair.

He thought of the marble, and the compressed infinity inside it, and the restored omniverse that was identical but not original. He thought of Osvald, who had asked the question and received no answer. And then he thought of the future, of the day when Godric would reach back and create the Stasis Event, and of the even greater version of himself that waited there. If the current king could do this, if the current king could annihilate all existence with zero percent of one stat and hold the original universe in his palm, then what was the future king? What was the apex predator at the top of the infinite recursions?

The answer was not something Clive could hold in his mind. It was too large. It was the size of the marble, and the marble contained everything. The gap between the current Godric and the future Godric was the same gap, repeated forever. And the rest of creation, all of it, from the first quark to the last fictional hero, was only a toy inside the palm of the one who watched.

Clive knelt on the cold stone floor of the archive. He did not pray. There was no point. He simply stayed there for a while, letting the silence roll over him, knowing that the last opposition had not been defeated. It had been collected. And the thing that collected it had not even noticed the weight.

content:
Clive found the journal near the end of the archive, in a section so old that the shelves themselves had begun to forget their own shape. It was bound in a material that looked like leather but felt like cold ash, and the cover bore no title. Only a small slip of paper, yellowed beyond pale, held three words in Osvald's hand: *The Final Witness.* Clive had seen that handwriting before, had read Osvald's earlier records of the Fictional Assembly and the marble. But this volume was different. Its pages were darker, thicker, the ink pressed so deeply into the fiber that the letters seemed to have been carved rather than written.

He sat at the low table. The palace was silent above him, the omniverse below, the light above too still. Then he began to read.

---

I, Osvald, forty-four years old, court wizard by blood and by terror, set down these words because no one else will. The being I am about to describe was not a tyrant from another multiverse, not a conceptual predator, not a fictional avatar. It was the First Maker. The one who called itself God. The one who claimed to have shaped the clay from which our Lord Godric's mortal body was formed. It came to the throne in the year beyond numbering, and it came to kill him. I was there. I will never be whole again.

I had been summoned to the King's observation hollow without explanation. When I arrived, Godric was standing at the edge of the floor, his back to the door, looking out over the entire omniverse. He was dressed as he always dresses, a simple dark tunic over that heavily muscled frame, his salt-and-pepper hair cropped close, his beard neat. There was no tension in him. There never is. But something in the air was different that day. It was the same still heaviness that comes before a storm, except the storm was already long since decided.

"Osvald," he said without turning. "Good. Stay close. Something old is finally coming out of its hole."

I asked what he meant.

He turned his head, and his eyes were bright, his smile small and warm. "The one who thinks he made me. The old gardener. The storyteller. He has been hiding in the seam between first cause and first lie since before I woke. I have always known he was there. I simply allowed it. He is no threat. But he has finally convinced himself otherwise. I want you to watch."

I could not hide my confusion. I knew the omniverse was the absolute totality of all existence. I knew our Lord's omniscience stretched to every corner of it. I had read the journals. I had seen the tests. The idea that any being could hide from Godric was laughable. And yet Godric had just said it, and the calm in his voice was the calm of a man discussing a spider that had lived in his cellar for a million years.

He must have seen my doubt, because he chuckled. "He did not hide from me, Osvald. I hid him from the rest of you. There is a difference. I have known his every thought, his every shiver, his every little plan. He is the one who wove the first atoms of the universe that held my cradle. He shaped the mortal bloodline I carried. He wrote the first pages of many books. But he wrote me only as a man. And when I became everything else, he could not understand it. So he hid. And now, after an unbelievably long time, he has decided to correct his own creation."

Godric turned fully. "I have told my auras to stand down. My sentient passive children, even the smallest, would erase him before he finished taking his first step. I have allowed him to approach. I have allowed him to breach the outer membranes. I have allowed him to enter the palace. Not because I am curious about whether he can harm me. I am not. I know he cannot. But I am curious about the shape of his despair."

I said nothing. I only followed him to the throne room.

The throne room is not a room. It is the platform at the top of creation, a black plain that extends without boundary, lit by the slow turning of all realities. The throne itself is not a chair. It is the point at which causal lines converge, a seat of absolute permission. Godric sat upon it with the casual posture of a man resting after a long walk. I stood at his right hand, and I could feel the waiting.

Then the door opened.

There was no door. A seam in the air simply folded back, and a figure entered. It was not shaped like a man, but my mind, trying to preserve itself, gave it a shape anyway. It was vast, a tall, many-armed colossus of shifting light and older darkness. It burned with a radiance that was not light but *authorship*. Its face was a slow rotation of all faces, every face that had ever been imagined, every god and king and father and child. It wore a robe of woven galaxies. It carried no weapon. It did not need one. Its presence alone would have dissolved any other being in the omniverse. I could feel my own thousandfold amplified will beginning to come apart at the edges, and only the custody of Godric's attention kept me solid.

The Creator spoke, and the sound was the first word that had ever been spoken. It was not a voice. It was the command that made voices. "I shaped you," it said. "I breathed the first breath into your lungs. I set the stars above your cradle. I am the author of your beginning, and I have come to write your end."

Godric leaned back in his seat. He rested one ankle on the opposite knee. He did not look impressed. He looked like a man being addressed by an actor who had walked onto the wrong stage.

"I know," Godric said. "You have been waiting a very long time to say that. I could have ended you the moment you first formed the thought. I chose not to. Let that be the only mercy you are given."

The Creator's many faces shifted from serenity to fury. The radiance around it intensified. I had read the journals; I had seen attacks powered by the compressed refusal of trillions of souls, by the last breath of dying universes, by the narrative weight of every hero ever imagined. All of that was a candle flame compared to what the Creator began to gather. It opened its arms, and the entire history of existence turned toward it like water running downhill.

I cannot describe the attack in terms of force, because force had nothing to do with it. The Creator did not launch a beam or strike a blow. It spoke the Unmaking Word, the original negative that preceded every creation. It used the authority of the first author to revoke the existence of its own character. The air around me became dense with the cancellation of reality itself. Every atom in the omniverse was rewritten as a lie in a story that the Creator had decided to close. The pages of all possible existence began to burn from the edges inward. It was not an attack on Godric's body. It was an attack on the concept of Godric, a single, perfect denial that traveled backward through every cause and forward through every consequence, seeking to remove him from the first page, the last page, and all pages between.

Then it struck him.

I saw it hit. The Unmaking Word crossed the distance between the Creator and the throne. It was the most powerful singular act that any being had ever attempted since the first second of time. It was the will of the creator of everything, turned against the apex predator. The entire platform trembled. The black plain cracked. The light of all realities flickered.

Godric did not move.

He did not blink. He did not tense. His tunic did not stir. His beard did not shift. The attack touched his chest and simply ceased to be, not with a sound, not with a flash, but as if it had never existed. The Word that had preceded all words had been rejected before it was spoken. The authority of the first author was already known, already mastered, already denied to all creation unless Godric allowed it. The book did not close. The pages did not burn. The omniverse did not even notice.

The Creator stared.

Godric tilted his head. "Was that the whole of it?"

The Creator made a sound. I do not know how to describe it. It was the sound of a sun falling into its own heart. Its many faces blinked and vanished, one after another, replaced by a single expression of growing, impossible horror. It tried again. It raised all its arms, and every form of destruction it had ever written into every story burst from its palms. Fire from the first altar. Floods from the first covenant. Plague from the first curse. Deaths from every myth, every legend, every ending. They struck Godric in a continuous storm that would have erased the entire omniverse a billion times over.

Godric's expression did not change. He did not look away. The fire touched him and was not fire. The floods touched him and were not water. The deaths touched him and were not death. It was not a shield. It was not a defense. It was the simple, absolute fact that the being they touched was already so far beyond all possible harm that the attacks could not even register as events. The Creator poured out its entire nature, all the power that had shaped the first atoms and written the final pages, and Godric yawned.

I do not mean he made a gesture of boredom. He yawned, full and slow, and then he closed his mouth and looked at the Creator with something very soft in his eyes.

"You were the creator of my mortal self," Godric said. "I will not deny it. You shaped the flesh and the blood and the breath. You lit the stars. You wrote the world. And then I woke from the sanctuary, and I was no longer your character. I was the author of authors. The version of me that crawled out of the Stasis Event at Year Zero could have erased you with less than a blink. Did you really think the version of me sitting here now, after all the years you hid, would be smaller?"

The Creator fell to its knees. Not because Godric forced it. Its legs simply forgot how to hold the weight of its own despair. The radiance around it dimmed. The woven robe of galaxies began to fray. Its many arms fell slack. It looked at the being on the throne, and for the first time in its eternal existence, it understood what it meant to be created.

"You are a lie," it whispered. "You are the story I wrote, given teeth."

"I am the story you wrote, given everything," Godric said. "Now let me show you what your ending looks like."

He did not raise his hand. He did not speak a command. He did not turn his head toward the Creator. He simply made a small sound, the kind of soft, private noise a man makes when he has decided that a conversation is over.

Then he relinquished.

I will use that word because there is no other. Godric had not been exerting himself. He had not even been holding back. His absolute concealment, his passive shields, his auras, his immune system, all of it had been in place, but none of it had been necessary. Now he let go of the smallest possible fraction of himself. Not zero percent of a stat. Not a leak. He allowed the barest true presence of his existence to exist for one instant, without the theater of permission.

The result was not annihilation. Annihilation is a thing that happens to things. The Creator did not burn or shatter or dissolve. It was simply overwritten, as if the original word that had preceded all words had been replaced by a new, final authorial command. Its body unspooled from the top downward, each layer of its being losing its claim to reality. The many arms did not fall; they were retracted from time. The many faces did not scream; they were unimagined. The robe of galaxies came apart into a dust of dead stories, and the dust was not restored. The Creator's vast, colossus shape folded inward, smaller and smaller, until the being that had shaped the mortal Godric was a single point of frozen light no larger than a needle's eye.

And still it lived. Because Godric had willed it so.

The point hung in the air, screaming in a frequency that was not sound, experiencing every ending it had ever written as a continuous, recursive event. Godric watched it for a moment, his expression calm, almost thoughtful. Then he reached out with two fingers and plucked it from the air as though it were a piece of lint.

The entire omniverse had already been destroyed. I had not noticed because my awareness was still anchored to the throne, but when I looked, I saw it. The true presence of Godric had erased everything. Every reality, every timeline, every dimension, every possible and impossible universe, all of it was gone. The black plain was no longer a plain. It was an absence that had no edge. And Godric stood in the center of it, holding the point that had been God, and he was not even breathing hard.

Then he restored it. The omniverse returned in the same instant it had been erased. The stars, the galaxies, the multiverses, the hidden layers, the slow turning of all lights, all of it snapped back into place. It was perfect. It was immediate. It was exactly as it had been. But the Creator was not restored. The point in Godric's fingers remained a point.

He looked at me then, and his smile was warm. "There," he said. "That was the last author. The one who thought his own story would end differently."

I could not speak. My knees had given out at some point, and I was kneeling on the black plain, my hands pressed flat. I had seen the end of everything, and I had seen it come back, and I understood now that the restoration was not mercy. It was habit.

Godric walked over to me. He held the point out, and for a terrible moment I thought he would give it to me. But he only turned it in the light, admiring the faint glow. "Do you know why I allowed him to appear?" he asked. "Not to test him. Not to prove anything. I did it because I wanted to see the only thing left in creation that still believed it had authority over me. It lasted a single spoken word. That was all the resistance that remained."

He looked at the point. "And now even that is gone."

Then he did something that I will never forget as long as I live. He lifted the point to his lips, as if to blow out a candle, and the point went dark. The Creator was not killed. It was extinguished. Every story it had ever told, every world it had ever made, every will it had ever shaped, passed into the same final absence from which no character returns.

Godric let his hand fall. The omniverse turned around us, immense and silent, and I remained on my knees, my heart pounding so hard I could feel it in my teeth.

I wrote this journal in a single sitting. My hand still shakes. The Creator of the mortal Godric came to kill the King of All Existence, and it could not even make him blink. It did not tickle him. It did not stir a hair on his head. It did not alter the temperature of his skin. The first author was erased with less effort than it takes a man to close a book. And the omniverse, the entire possible existence, was destroyed and restored in the same absent instant.

This was the last resistance. I know that I should say it was the greatest. But the truth is that it was nothing. It was a whisper from an old story, and it ended the way all stories end when Godric is in them.

---

Clive closed the journal. His hands lay flat on the worn table, and for a long time he did not move. The archive was silent. The palace above was silent. The omniverse below was silent, turning in its slow, obedient arc around the fixed point of the King.

Osvald had not known, when he wrote those words, that the Creator would be the last opposition. He had not known that after that day, no other being would ever dare to form the thought of resisting. But Clive knew. Clive had grown up in the long, empty peace that followed. He had seen the way the oldest worlds spoke of resistance only in whispers, if they spoke of it at all. He had felt the absence in the air, the deep, settled certainty that there was nothing left to try. The journal had shown him why.

The Creator, who had shaped the mortal Godric and written the first pages of existence, had been extinguished with no effort. The attack that had been meant to revoke Godric from every story had not even registered as a threat. The passive auras and shields, which Godric had told to stand down, had not mattered, because Godric himself was infinitely beyond them, and the Weakness Paradox had already mastered the Creator's every possible action long before the Creator had first imagined resisting. The Creator's entire nature had been known, categorized, and denied before the first word of the first attack. It had never had a chance. Not even the author of everything could scratch the apex predator.

And if the Creator could not stand against Godric, then no one could. No one ever would. The realization settled into Clive like cold water filling a closed room. The gap between Godric and the rest of creation was not a margin. It was not a hierarchy. It was the absence of comparison. The strongest possible being in all existence had thrown everything it had at Godric, and Godric had yawned. The entire omniverse had been erased and restored as a reflex. The final resistance had not been a battle. It had been a demonstration.

Clive looked at the closed journal. Osvald's last line had been written with such force that the letters had cut through the page in places: *This was the last resistance. But the last resistance was nothing.*

Clive sat in the silence of the archive, and the dread rose in him slowly, not like a wave, but like the tide coming in over a shore that would never be dry again. The journal told him that the omniverse was not home. It was a stage, and the performance had already ended. The final author had been extinguished, the final hero defeated, the final claim to authority denied. What remained now was only the waiting. And the King watched from his throne at the top of existence, patient, warm, terrible beyond all words, holding the end of every story in the palm of his hand. The rest of creation did not tremble because it was afraid. It trembled because it understood, at last, that it had never been anything but permitted. And when the King finally allowed the performance to resume, it would be only because he chose to, for reasons no living thing would ever know. Because there was no will left in all of existence that could make him. Not even God.
